rationale: The judgment changed, so a complete assessment is returned. Two grades in the incumbent violated the anchor-only rule as it now reads (review note #319): TIK-C029 (ergometrine persisting after peptide hydrolysis) has no admitted evidence record — the second reader found TIK-E038 does not bear on it — and was nonetheless graded provisionally supported on its anchor; it is now unresolved at low confidence and told in the article as what the paper reports. TIK-C033 (a gram of ergot reaches the minimum effective LSA dose) was likewise carried on its anchor; it now rests on a separately disclosed basis — TIK-E008, which records the measured yield of 0.54 and 0.48 mg per gram and the authors' one-gram extrapolation — while the half-milligram threshold remains anchor-only, so the grade is weakly supported at low confidence rather than provisionally supported. TIK-C034 (Claviceps paspali hosts naturalized in Europe only in the nineteenth century) is added to the featured set: anchor-only and graded unresolved, it is nonetheless a rung the mechanism stands on, since it closes the one alternative ergot route and leaves purpurea-plus-lye as the only pathway on the table; a reader should see that the choice of pathway is itself a claim. The steelman is rewritten: the incumbent's version stated the initiates' formula ('I fasted, I drank the kykeon') as placing the drink at the end of a fast, a reading of a text no admitted record holds, now written as the proponents' reading, and each remaining premise now names the evidence record that carries it. Case verdict (mixed), the load-bearing set, and the remaining fifteen claim verdicts stand; weakest links gain TIK-C033. The article is the incumbent's telling with three local edits — the ergometrine sentence, the dose paragraph, and one sentence for the paspali point — and no other growth; the inherited-sacrament account is told as strong and weak variants of one account, matching the accounts field. The question and accounts are kept. No research item is settled: the Pontós chapters, the Gainsford post, and the Bremmer text all failed retrieval this pass, so every item stays open and the crux order is unchanged.
article:
In September 2020, a lawyer with degrees in classics published a book arguing that Western civilization's central rite began as a drug. Brian Muraresku's *The Immortality Key* spent weeks on the bestseller lists and revived a hypothesis that mainstream classics had spent forty years declining: that the kykeon — the barley drink of the Eleusinian Mysteries, the initiation Pindar and Cicero link with knowledge of death and what follows it — was a psychedelic, and that the earliest Greek-speaking Christians inherited a version of it as the original Eucharist. A “religion with no name,” running beneath the official ones, with a spiked cup as its sacrament.

The thesis sounds like one claim. It is a ladder of them, and the state of the evidence changes drastically from rung to rung. The bottom has been settled by laboratory chemistry within the last six years. The top is contradicted by the earliest documents we have. The rungs in between — the ones the book actually stands on — turn on a handful of physical tests that, remarkably, nobody has ever run.

## Five accounts of one cup

Before the evidence, the contenders. Five serious accounts are in play, and they do not sort neatly into “for” and “against.”

- **The drugged kykeon.** Ergot growing on the sanctuary's barley, processed in wood-ash lye, supplied lysergamides related to LSD; the initiates' visions were pharmacological. It predicts ergot-derived alkaloids in Eleusinian drinking vessels, and a preparation that reliably gives a profound, mostly positive experience at a dose one person could be served.
- **The ritual machine.** Days of fasting, procession, secrecy, darkness and light, ritual drama and mass emotion in a hall built for the purpose were enough on their own. The kykeon was what its recipe says. It predicts cereal and mint in the cups and nothing else — and a modern literature showing that drug-free ritual can produce experiences of the reported intensity.
- **A phenomenon that may not need explaining.** The “life-changing vision” both sides argue over may itself be a modern reading of a few ancient lines about afterlife hopes. If no ancient text attests a transformative experience *during* initiation, the drug-versus-ritual argument has nothing to explain. It predicts that a philological audit will find the beatific vision to be a twentieth-century construction.
- **The inherited sacrament.** Dionysian wine carried the pharmacology; the Gospel of John paints Jesus in Dionysian colors; the earliest Greek-speaking Christians drank a drugged Eucharist later suppressed by the Church Fathers. In its author's own scholarly register this shrinks to a weaker form — *some* early community, somewhere, spiked its cup — and this article treats the two as strong and weak versions of one account. It predicts psychoactive residues in securely identified early-Christian vessels and a traceable chain from mystery cult to church.
- **The Jewish table.** The Eucharist descends from Second-Temple meal blessings — the thanksgiving over bread and cup — exactly as the earliest texts present it, and its wine symbolism needs no drug. It predicts what the Didache and Justin Martyr describe: bread, wine with water, thanksgiving, and a hostile stance toward pagan mysteries.

In every case, what would decide between them is a measurement or an audit that has not been made. That is the strangest feature of this controversy, and the reason it belongs on this site.

## What the chemistry has settled

Start with what is no longer worth arguing about. For most of the twentieth century, claims about ancient drug use ran on iconography and inference — a mushroom-shaped carving here, a poppy goddess there — and could be dismissed accordingly. Residue chemistry ended that era. On the altars of an eighth-century BCE Judahite shrine at Tel Arad, cannabis burned with animal dung. In human hair from a Bronze Age cult cave on Menorca, measured directly in the tissue: ephedrine, atropine, scopolamine. In a Ptolemaic Egyptian mug shaped like the god Bes, a fermented multi-plant preparation including harmal and blue lotus — though the mug was bought on the Cairo art market, so its chemistry is stronger than its provenance. At a California rock-art site, chewed wads of hallucinogenic Datura tucked into ceiling cracks. [People in the ancient world really did take mind-altering substances in religious settings]{claim=TIK-C001}: that is now direct chemical fact, several times over, from independent teams on independent materials.

{plate:IMG-TIK-P01}

The first-century pharmacopeia points the same way for wine. Dioscorides, as Muraresku summarizes him, describes [wines deliberately compounded with psychoactive plants]{claim=TIK-C002} — henbane, mandrake, black nightshade, this last credited with producing “not unpleasant visions” — and Greek routinely called wine a *pharmakon*, a drug. The summary is a proponent's and the exact passages remain to be pulled, but the capability is not seriously in dispute. These were medical recipes with stated indications; nothing in them makes a drug-wine a sacrament.

So the floor of the ladder holds. The trouble — the reason this case exists — is that the floor is routinely presented as if it supported the penthouse. A cannabis altar in Iron Age Judah is excellent evidence that ancient ritual pharmacology existed. It is no evidence that ergot was in the cup at Eleusis, and less than none that a Christian in Corinth drank it. Every rung must pay its own way.

## The drink with a published recipe

Antiquity left one recipe for the kykeon. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter — the founding myth of the Mysteries — the grieving goddess refuses red wine and asks instead for [barley meal and water mixed with soft pennyroyal mint]{claim=TIK-C003}. That is the whole list. No ancient source names ergot; none describes a processing step beyond mixing; the drink reads as a rustic barley posset with an aromatic herb. The Hymn is a myth, not a liturgical manual, and the cult was secret by law, so the silence is not proof. But everything psychoactive in the modern hypothesis is an addition to this text, not a reading of it.

{plate:IMG-TIK-P02}

The hypothesis's founders knew this and built on it anyway, because of what barley implies. Ergot, the fungus *Claviceps purpurea*, grows on cereal grains, and its alkaloids are chemical cousins of LSD, which Albert Hofmann first synthesized from ergot derivatives. In 1978 Hofmann, with the mushroom pioneer R. Gordon Wasson and the classicist Carl Ruck, proposed in *The Road to Eleusis* that ergot on the barley of the Rarian plain supplied the kykeon's secret — while conceding, in Hofmann's words, “We have no way to tell what the chemistry was of the ergot of barley or wheat raised on the Rarian plain.” In 2000 Ruck and two collaborators sharpened the idea: hydrolyze the toxic alkaloids in alkali and a safer, psychoactive preparation might result. Classics mostly declined the whole line, and it hibernated in the entheogen literature until Muraresku's book brought it back with two genuinely new kinds of support.

{plate:IMG-TIK-P03}

## The two best cards in the Greek hand

The first is archaeological, and it is the case's one hard physical datum. At Mas Castellar de Pontós in Catalonia — near the ancient Greek colony of Emporion, at a site with a sanctuary linked to Demeter and Persephone — a 2002 analysis reported [fragments of ergot inside a ceremonial vessel and in the dental calculus of a young man buried there]{claim=TIK-C004}. Substance, ingestion, and cult context together, in a Greek-influenced setting. It is the closest thing the hypothesis has to a smoking gun, and its limitations are as large as they sound. It is one analysis, performed twenty-four years ago and never independently replicated, at a site a thousand kilometers from Eleusis. This case has so far read it only through the 2026 chemistry paper's citation; even the Demeter-and-Persephone attribution of the sanctuary rests on an excavation report not yet opened. Retellings have a documented habit of hardening “fragments of ergot” into “hallucinogenic alkaloids chemically detected,” which the primary wording, as quoted, does not say. And there is a quieter problem: ergot is what barley carries. A barley vessel with ergot in it is, absent more, a barley vessel. Whether the 2002 report compared the vessel and the teeth against grain from the site's own mills and storage pits — the contrast that would lift the find above background — is exactly what reading the primary chapters would settle. Other ergot finds are reported in secondary surveys, in a Bronze Age cult area in Apulia, an Iron Age grave in Poland, the gut of a Danish bog body; none has been opened by this case, and none is a Demeter sanctuary.

{plate:IMG-TIK-P04}

The second card is chemical, and it arrived in February 2026. The standing objection to the ergot hypothesis was always toxicity: raw ergot causes ergotism — gangrene, convulsions — not transcendence. A team including Ruck and members of an entheogen-research center finally ran the 2000 proposal. Across forty-eight experiments they refluxed powdered ergot in wood-ash lye, the strong alkali ancient Greeks could make, and showed that [the toxic ergopeptides can be hydrolyzed completely while measurable amounts of the psychoactive lysergamides LSA and iso-LSA appear]{claim=TIK-C005} — about half a milligram of each per gram of ergot. “Ergot would have poisoned everybody” is no longer available as an objection at the level of possibility.

Read the fine print, though, and the experiment cuts both ways. [Complete detoxification happened only at the harshest setting — the strongest lye, the lowest ergot loading, and at least two hours of controlled hot reflux]{claim=TIK-C028}; weaker or shorter treatments left poison detectable. The feasible pathway is therefore a *technology* — a specific, careful, multi-hour alkaline operation — and no ancient source attests anything of the kind at Eleusis. The authors are candid that “the focus of the study was to demonstrate the feasibility of this transformation,” not its history. Nor, the paper reports, did the process yield clean lysergamides: [ergometrine and its epimer remained detectable after the peptide alkaloids were gone]{claim=TIK-C029}. That sentence is told here as what the paper reports and nothing more: the ledger holds it on the claim's own anchor, with no admitted evidence record quoting the passage, and a proposition held that way is graded unresolved, not provisionally true. If it stands, its pharmacological weight is this case's note, not the paper's — ergometrine is an active ergot alkaloid in its own right — and belongs to a profile of the whole preparation that no one has run. The paper also reports, on a point likewise held only on its anchor, that [the host grasses of Claviceps paspali, a related ergot species, became naturalized in Europe only in the nineteenth century]{claim=TIK-C034}; were that admitted, the barley fungus and its lye processing would be the only ergot route left on the table. The result has also not been independently replicated, which matters more than usual because the hands were sympathetic ones — the hypothesis's co-originator among the authors, a twenty-six-year-old proposal finally validated by its proposer. Real chemistry, published in full, that a disinterested laboratory should now repeat on blinded ergot.

Then there is the gap between a molecule and a night. The yield is on the record: about half a milligram of each lysergamide per gram of ergot. From it the authors extrapolate that [about a gram of processed ergot per initiate would reach the literature's minimum effective dose of LSA]{claim=TIK-C033} — an arithmetic step, resting on a half-milligram threshold the paper cites from the pharmacological literature and this ledger has not yet admitted, so the step is held here as weakly supported, and a minimum in any case. “Related to LSD” carries the popular story, but LSA is substantially weaker than LSD, and the human literature on it — dominated by morning-glory-seed exposures — is a record of [hallucinations and euphoria mixed with sedation, nausea, autonomic effects, and anxiety]{claim=TIK-C006}. The 2026 authors propose that the pennyroyal in the recipe might smooth and extend the effect, and mark the idea as untested. Whether the full reconstructed preparation, at an achievable dose, reliably delivers the best night of a life rather than an unpleasant, queasy one is a question nobody has put to the extract itself.

## The empty cell

{plate:IMG-TIK-P05}

Here is the strangest fact in the whole controversy, and both sides agree on it: **no vessel from Eleusis has ever been chemically analyzed.** Not one. The 2026 paper says so while calling for exactly that analysis — the absence “is not decisive, since no systematic research has ever been conducted or since permission for such has never been granted.” Two millennia of cult, an excavated sanctuary, storerooms of curated ceramics — and the decisive measurement has never been made. Proponents read the blank as “not yet tested”; skeptics as “nothing found.” It is an untested absence, and it leaves [the headline Greek claim — deliberately prepared ergot in the Eleusinian kykeon]{claim=TIK-C007} — with real circumstantial scaffolding and an empty cell where its direct evidence should be.

The scaffolding should not be oversold, and the counter-record is specific. The canonical recipe names nothing psychoactive. The sanctuary's finances were carved on stone and publicly audited; Kevin Clinton, who has spent a career on the Eleusinian inscriptions, notes that the accounts track the sacred grain into sacrifices and dedications, “none of it for the production of ergot or drugs.” A secret ingredient gathered free from the field would not appear in accounts, so the silence is not fatal — but it is a specific, published, audited silence rather than a general one. And the methodological critics have a point this case adopts as a rule: the literature from *The Road to Eleusis* onward shows “a pattern of presenting claims, followed by mild circumstantial evidence, rhetorically solidifying the interpretation of this evidence into a ‘fact,’ on which is built each subsequent round of conjecture.” Possibility must not be promoted into fact and then load-borne.

Beneath the attribution question sits the one that gives it its point: [did the initiates' experience require a drug at all]{claim=TIK-C008}? Modern trials show that pharmacologically occasioned mystical-type experience is real — psilocybin, in a 2006 double-blind study, produced experiences volunteers rated months later among the most significant of their lives. That proves the pharmacological route exists; it does not prove Eleusis used it. The ritual account needs no supply chain, no dosing control, and no secret technology, and it ran stable for nearly two thousand years. Yet the ritual account is asserted more often than it is evidenced, and its canonical statements have not been audited here. The 2026 authors, for their part, call the Mysteries' psychedelic core “reasonably certain” on the strength of “numerous accounts of the experience” — accounts they do not quote or locate beyond Pindar and Cicero, who, as cited, link initiation with knowledge of death and the afterlife rather than describe an experience in the hall. That opens the third account: whether any ancient text, read without the lens of Carl Kerényi's twentieth-century reading of a passage in Plato's *Phaedrus*, attests a transformative experience during initiation at all. If none does, both the drug and the ritual accounts are explaining a phenomenon a modern scholar built.

## The Christian half, where the ladder thins

The book's second act needs the practice to cross into Christianity, and the crossing is argued through Dionysus. [The Gospel of John engages Dionysian imagery]{claim=TIK-C009} — water into wine at Cana, “I am the true vine” — and some serious scholars read those passages as deliberately painting Jesus in the wine god's colors; others read the same passages as Jewish messianic abundance. Either way, a literary relationship is a claim about texts. To get pharmacology across, the Dionysian wine must have been psychedelic — Muraresku himself, at Harvard, called that “a big if” — and then an actual community must have transferred the practice, not just the imagery. He names the next gap himself: “Where are the drugs?”

What the early Christian record shows is a Jewish table. The earliest descriptions of the Eucharist we possess — Paul's, the Didache's prayers, Justin Martyr's account around 155 CE — describe bread and a cup of wine (Justin: “wine mixed with water”) in thanksgiving form. The Didache gives thanks “for the holy vine of David”; Justin addresses the pagan parallels directly and runs the borrowing the other way, calling the Mithraic meal something “wicked devils have imitated.” The nearest thing to a drugged cup anywhere in the record is hostile: Irenaeus's polemic against the Gnostic Marcus, accused of a conjuring trick that turned the cup “a purple and reddish color” and of compounding love-philters — fraud and seduction, not sacramental psychedelia. On the current documentary record, [the claim that the original Eucharist was a psychedelic potion]{claim=TIK-C011} is contradicted. [The weaker claim that some early community, somewhere, spiked its cup]{claim=TIK-C010} is neither supported nor refuted, because — the pattern by now is familiar — **no securely identified early-Christian liturgical vessel has ever been chemically tested either.**

{plate:IMG-TIK-P06}

The experts the book leans on are blunt. Patrick McGovern, the Penn Museum's pioneer of biomolecular archaeology and an adviser Muraresku consulted, calls the scientific evidence connecting psychedelics to early Christianity “extremely weak to nonexistent.” Jan Bremmer, the mystery-cult specialist: “Christianity was not a mystery cult.” Bart Ehrman: not plausible. Sympathetic readers cut the same way — Jerry Brown, himself a psychedelic-Christianity author, concludes the book “fails to make a compelling case for its grand theory,” presenting speculation as fact. And Muraresku's scholarly register concedes more than his marketing: he does not defend a psychedelic Last Supper (“I don't hang my hat on that claim”), and his own site grants that “the smoking gun remains elusive.”

That transmission rung — [a psychoactive sacrament actually passing from the Greek mysteries into the Christian cup]{claim=TIK-C012} — is the weakest load-bearing element in the structure. Cultural contact is real; wine-and-immortality symbolism is shared; and none of that needs transmission to explain, because wine and immortality are among the commonest religious symbols of the ancient Mediterranean. Beneath it sits a framework — [the Eucharist as an outgrowth of pagan mystery ritual rather than Jewish meal practice]{claim=TIK-C013} — that the relevant specialist fields reject. If the framework is wrong, any future psychedelic Christian cup would have to establish its own transmission vector rather than inherit one.

## The money, and a disclosure

The hypothesis now has institutional machinery. The Yale Ancient Pharmacology Program, supported by the Athanatos Foundation Muraresku founded, is building the residue-analysis capacity this case's decisive tests require; the funder's page says the project “reframes our understanding of early Christian ritual and its pharmacological roots,” language that appears there and not in the program's scientific papers. Its published funding statement names its supporters: E. Jhong, the Robert and MeiLi Hefner Foundation, the Athanatos Foundation, and B. Muraresku.

E. Jhong is this project's founder. Readers should weigh that: the program best positioned to test the Eleusinian and early-Christian claims is funded by the hypothesis's author, his foundation, and the founder of the site you are reading. Funding is provenance, not refutation — chemistry stands or falls on replication, not on who paid for the instrument — but independence accounting is half of this case's method, and it must include ourselves. Any future YAPP result entering this ledger carries that flag. The same discipline runs in reverse: critics' motives are context, never evidence about what was in an ancient cup.

## Where this case stands, and what would move it

Rung by rung: ancient ritual pharmacology, established. Feasible ergot chemistry, demonstrated once, under demanding conditions, by interested hands, awaiting replication. Ergot at Eleusis, weakly supported — one unreplicated Iberian analogue not yet read at its source, a workable mechanism, an empty cell at the sanctuary. The drug-versus-ritual question, unresolved, with the phenomenon itself now under audit. A psychedelic original Eucharist, contradicted by every early document. A spiked cup somewhere in early Christianity, untested. Transmission, the grand thesis, running on symbolism and possibility.

What would change our mind is concrete, and cheap. The vessels exist and the methods are routine — the same panels that found cannabis at Arad and alkaloids in Menorcan hair. Residue analysis of curated Eleusinian ceramics would move the case more than everything published since 1978, provided it targets the right molecules: the research item proposing the test argues that ergot lipids, which residue chemists have read as a marker that *cereal* was in a pot, would only report “barley was here” in any kykeon vessel — a premise this ledger has not verified, since the 2018 Pontós study behind it could not be checked against its text this pass; the discriminating targets it names are LSA, iso-LSA and lysergic acid above soil background, with a lipid test as the cereal control. A lysergamide hit in a series of Eleusinian cups would make the drugged kykeon the best-evidenced claim of its kind anywhere; a cereal-positive, lysergamide-negative series would be the first genuine null at the sanctuary. Reading the 2002 Pontós chapters, and re-analyzing the samples, would decide whether the case's one physical datum is diagnostic or background. A disinterested laboratory repeating the lye chemistry on blinded ergot, and a pharmacological profile of the whole extract, would close or reopen the mechanism. A preregistered survey of early-Christian vessels — preregistered because the likeliest laboratory is an interested one — would convert the Christian half from analogy to measurement, in either direction. And a philological audit of the testimonia would tell us whether there was ever a vision to explain. The full agenda, ranked by what each test would settle, is below.

assessment.synthesis: The ladder does not fail uniformly, so the roll-up stays mixed rather than collapsing to one grade. The observation rung is solid: ritual psychoactive use is established by independent residue chemistry (TIK-E001, TIK-E002, TIK-E003, TIK-E004), compounded drug-wines are attested at second hand (TIK-E005), and the Hymn's recipe is what it says (TIK-E006). None of that discriminates between the accounts. The mechanism rung moved once, with the 48-run hydrolysis experiment (TIK-E008), and the preprint fine print (TIK-E038) fixes how narrowly: complete detoxification only at pH 12.5, 5% w/v, 120 minutes. That retires 'ergot means ergotism' at the level of possibility while raising the historical cost — a controlled technology no source attests. Two propositions the paper also reports — residual ergometrine (TIK-C029) and the late naturalization of Claviceps paspali hosts (TIK-C034) — are held on their anchors alone with no admitted record and are graded unresolved; the one-gram dose step (TIK-C033) rests on the measured yield in TIK-E008 but on an unadmitted dose threshold, so it is weakly supported, and the pharmacological question (TIK-E012, TIK-E013) stays open. The attribution rung splits. At Eleusis the decisive cell is empty, not negative (TIK-E009); TIK-C007 sits at weakly_supported, propped by one unreplicated Iberian find seen only through citation (TIK-E007) and pressed by the silent recipe (TIK-E015), the audited accounts (TIK-E016) and the methodological critique (TIK-E019). Beneath it the generator claim TIK-C008 is doubly unresolved: no record evidences ritual sufficiency, and the proponents' premise rests on 'numerous accounts' they do not cite (TIK-E040, TIK-E041), so whether there is a phenomenon to explain is itself under audit. On the Christian side the record is contrary rather than empty: Justin and the Didache describe bread and wine in Jewish thanksgiving form (TIK-E022, TIK-E023), the one drugged-cup text is fraud polemic (TIK-E021), specialists reject the framework (TIK-E017, TIK-E018, TIK-E020), and the author declines the strong form (TIK-E024). The single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is TIK-E008: without it TIK-C005 reverts to a 26-year-old proposal, TIK-C028 and TIK-C033 lose their basis, TIK-C007 loses its only mechanism, and the Greek half slides from weakly_supported toward contradicted, pulling the case verdict with it. Independence discipline is unchanged: one performance of the chemistry by interested-network authors, one unreplicated Iberian datum, and a funding edge (TIK-E027) that includes this project's founder.
assessment.steelman: The Mysteries were secret by law, and every countervailing record in this ledger is an argument from silence in precisely the domain where silence is expected: the Hymn is a public myth (TIK-E006, TIK-E015), the accounts are public stone (TIK-E016), and neither would record a secret ingredient gathered free from the Rarian field and processed in a sanctuary that never published its rite. Meanwhile the hypothesis has been right both times it was checked. The one Demeter-and-Persephone-linked sanctuary whose vessel and worshipper have been examined reportedly showed ergot in the cup and in a man's teeth (TIK-E007); the one chemical test ever run on the mechanism came out positive under conditions Greek technology could supply, at a yield the authors calculate reaches an active dose from a gram of fungus (TIK-E008). Complex psychotropic ritual drinks are chemically real in the Hellenistic Mediterranean (TIK-E003); first-century pharmacology compounded visionary wines (TIK-E005); pharmacologically occasioned mystical experience is real (TIK-E013). Proponents read the initiates' formula as placing the drink at the end of a fast, the moment of maximal absorption and the moment a ritual designer would choose — their reading of a text, not a record this ledger holds. The skeptical account, by contrast, has never been tested at Eleusis at all: no cup, no null, no cereal-positive-lysergamide-negative series (TIK-E009). A hypothesis that predicts correctly whenever it is checked, against an alternative that has never been checked, deserves more than 'weakly supported.' This assessment does not answer that argument; it holds that two checks, one unreplicated and one unread at its source, cannot carry the weight, and that the untested cell is untested for both sides.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: In its strongest public form: the Eleusinian Mysteries administered a psychedelic kykeon whose active agent was lye-processed ergot; Dionysian ritual wine carried similar pharmacology; and the earliest Greek-speaking Christians inherited this 'religion with no name' as a drugged Eucharist later suppressed by the Church Fathers. The author's scholarly formulation is weaker — the Dionysian premise is 'a big if,' the Last Supper claim is not defended, and 'the smoking gun remains elusive' — so the claim exists in at least three strengths (marketing copy, popular interviews, scholarly concession). This case assesses the strong form, records the concessions as evidence, and treats 'some community spiked its cup' as the weak version of the inheritance account.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether ancient Mediterranean peoples used psychoactive plants ritually — post-2020 archaeochemistry settled that — nor, since 2026, over whether an ergot preparation could be detoxified with ancient technology under demanding conditions. The crux is five narrow cells: the empty record at Eleusis, where no vessel has ever been analyzed and both sides cite the absence; the canonical recipe, which names nothing psychoactive and no processing; the Pontós find, one unreplicated 2002 analysis seen only through citation, which may show no more than that barley carries ergot; the phenomenon itself, since whether any ancient text attests a transformative experience during initiation — rather than afterlife hopes read through a modern lens — is under audit; and the transmission vector into Christianity, where the earliest documents describe a Jewish table liturgy and no chain of pharmacological inheritance has been shown.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For the Greek half: organic residue analysis of securely contexted, curated Eleusinian vessels, targeting LSA, iso-LSA and lysergic acid above soil background with ergot lipids run only as a cereal control — so that a predictable 'barley was here' is not read as a hit and a null is informative — together with reading the 2002 Pontós chapters and re-analyzing the samples, and an independent, blinded replication of the lye chemistry plus a pharmacological profile of the whole extract, which would also settle the ergometrine and dose questions now held on anchors alone. For the phenomenon: a philological audit of Phaedrus 250b–c and the testimonia for any text independent of Kerényi's reading attesting an experience during initiation. For the Christian half: a preregistered residue survey of securely identified early-Christian liturgical vessels, where a documented null is nearly as informative as a hit; a positive would establish a practice somewhere, not the norm and not inheritance, which would further require an uncommon shared recipe appearing first in a mystery-cult vessel and later in a Christian one.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Eleusis produced its effect without pharmacology: fasting, procession, secrecy, darkness and light, ritual drama and collective emotion in an initiation hall — mechanisms mainstream scholarship considers sufficient and which kept the rite stable for nearly two millennia — and the 'life-changing vision' may in any case be a modern reading of ancient afterlife hopes rather than an attested experience. The kykeon was what its recipe says: barley meal, water, pennyroyal. Ancient drug-wines were medicine and sorcery, not mystery-cult sacraments. The Pontós ergot, if it survives re-analysis, is ergot on barley in a barley vessel unless the report shows a contrast with the site's grain, and attests at most an Iberian practice. The Eucharist descends from Second-Temple Jewish meal liturgy exactly as the Didache, Paul and Justin present it, and its wine symbolism needs no drug. This account's unpaid debt: nobody has tested the Eleusinian or early-Christian vessels that could falsify it, and its ritual-sufficiency premise is asserted more than evidenced.

components.label: Ancient ritual pharmacology (background rung)
components.note: Independent residue chemistry (TIK-E001–E004) and attested drug-wines (TIK-E005, TIK-E003); settles that the practice existed, discriminates nothing about Eleusis or the Eucharist.

components.label: Lye-processed ergot as a feasible psychoactive preparation
components.note: One 48-run performance (TIK-E008, TIK-E038) by interested-network authors, unreplicated; complete detoxification only under the harshest conditions. Residual ergometrine (TIK-C029) and the paspali-host point (TIK-C034) are anchor-only and unresolved.

components.label: Pharmacology of the reconstructed drink
components.note: LSA is psychoactive but weaker and messier than LSD (TIK-E012); the whole extract has never been profiled; the one-gram dose step rests on measured yield but an unadmitted threshold (TIK-C033).

components.label: Ergot in the Eleusinian kykeon
components.note: Empty cell at the sanctuary (TIK-E009); one unreplicated Iberian analogue read through citation (TIK-E007); silent recipe and audited accounts against (TIK-E015, TIK-E016).

components.label: Whether a drug was needed — and whether there is a phenomenon to explain
components.note: No record evidences ritual sufficiency; proponents' 'numerous accounts' uncited (TIK-E040, TIK-E041); the beatific vision itself under philological audit.

components.label: The Christian half: original Eucharist, mystery-cult framework, transmission
components.note: Earliest documents describe a Jewish table liturgy (TIK-E022, TIK-E023); the only drugged-cup text is fraud polemic (TIK-E021); specialists and the author's own concessions against (TIK-E017, TIK-E018, TIK-E020, TIK-E024). The weak form — some community spiked its cup — is untested, not refuted.

researchPriority.reason: The decisive measurements are cheap, routine, and unrun: curated Eleusinian and early-Christian vessels exist, the analytical panels are the ones already used at Arad and Menorca, and the case's one physical datum can be re-read at its source for the price of a library request. Few controversies on this site have so large a gap between what would settle them and what it would cost.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Four independent residue studies by unrelated teams on unrelated materials (TIK-E001 cannabis at Arad, TIK-E002 alkaloids in Menorcan hair, TIK-E003 the Bes vessel, TIK-E004 Datura quids), three of them strong; only the Bes vessel carries a provenance caveat.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient people really did use mind-altering plants in religious settings — proven chemically, several times over.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: True under every account; it raises the prior that a drugged sacrament is possible but says nothing about Eleusis, ergot, or Christianity.
treatment.strongestObjection: None of the finds is Greek, none involves ergot, and one (Pinwheel Cave) has no cultural link to the Mediterranean at all.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Contamination or retraction findings across several of the underlying studies
A base-rate survey (TIK-R008) showing such finds are vanishingly rare, which would not overturn the claim but would change how much each new find means

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E005 carries Dioscorides' visionary wine recipes only as the proponent's summary in a friendly venue, and TIK-E003 shows a complex fermented psychotropic preparation in a Hellenistic vessel of market provenance; capability is attested, but the exact Dioscorides passages have not been pulled.

treatment.plainLanguage: Greek and Roman doctors did compound wines with psychoactive plants.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Medical recipes with stated indications; they show a drug-wine was makeable, not that any cult served one.
treatment.strongestObjection: The record here is secondhand and therapeutic; nothing in it connects a drug-wine to a sacrament.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Pulling the Dioscorides passages (TIK-R006) and finding the summary overstates them
A ritual-context vessel with a compounded drug-wine residue, which would raise the claim's diagnosticity rather than its credibility

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E006 reads the passage directly: meal, water, soft mint, wine refused; no other ancient recipe is on record.

treatment.plainLanguage: The only ancient recipe for the kykeon is barley, water, and mint — nothing psychoactive.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both sides must explain it; it fits the ritual-machine account without addition and forces the drugged-kykeon account to posit a secret ingredient and a secret process.
treatment.strongestObjection: The Hymn is a myth, not a liturgy, and the cult was secret by law, so the recipe's silence is expected under either account.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Any ancient testimonium naming an additive or a processing step (TIK-R006)
Evidence that the Hymn's recipe reflects a different, non-Eleusinian kykeon tradition

claimAssessments.reasoning: One admitted record (TIK-E007), which carries the 2002 analysis only as cited by the 2026 paper; the primary chapters are unread and the source unverified, the analysis is unreplicated, and the sanctuary attribution rests on an excavation report not opened.

treatment.plainLanguage: At an Iberian site linked to the Eleusinian goddesses, ergot was reportedly found in a ritual cup and in a man's teeth.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only datum combining substance, ingestion and cult context — but a thousand kilometres from Eleusis, and ergot is what barley carries, so without a site-wide contrast it may be background.
treatment.strongestObjection: A barley vessel with ergot in it is, absent more, a barley vessel; no one has shown the report compared the finds against the site's own grain.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading the 2002 chapters (TIK-R010) and finding a documented contrast with mill and storage samples — upward
Modern re-analysis of the samples (TIK-R004) failing to confirm Claviceps, or the primary text proving weaker than the citation — downward

claimAssessments.reasoning: One weak record (TIK-E014), a proponent's summary of scholars who read John as Dionysian; the same scholarly literature names Jewish messianic-abundance readings, which no record in the ledger yet carries directly.

treatment.plainLanguage: John's Gospel may deliberately paint Jesus in the colours of the wine god Dionysus.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A claim about texts and symbols; even if true it carries no pharmacology across, as the proponent concedes.
treatment.strongestObjection: Water-into-wine and the true vine are at home in Jewish messianic imagery without any Dionysian reference.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An audit of the New Testament scholarship on both readings
Nothing about this claim would move the pharmacological claims either way

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E008 (strong) reports complete disappearance of the six toxic ergopeptides with LSA and iso-LSA at 0.54 and 0.48 mg/g over 48 runs; TIK-E038 (same performance) fixes the conditions; TIK-E010 and TIK-E011 are the proposal's lineage. Single performance by interested-network authors, no independent replication.

treatment.plainLanguage: Boiling ergot in wood-ash lye can destroy its poisons and leave LSD-related compounds behind — shown once, in a lab.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Removes the toxicity objection at the level of possibility, but the demanding conditions make the historical reconstruction require a technology no source attests.
treatment.strongestObjection: One experiment by the hypothesis's co-originator and an entheogen-research centre, under two hours of controlled reflux at the highest pH — feasibility in a modern lab, not evidence of ancient practice.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blinded independent replication (TIK-R002) — toward established
Replication failing or showing a narrow safety envelope — toward mixed, reopening the toxicity objection at practical strength

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E038 quotes the paper's statement of the conditions directly, and TIK-E008 on the parent claim records that lower pH or shorter treatments left ergopeptides detectable; a statement of what the paper reports, established by its text, from a single performance.

treatment.plainLanguage: Full detoxification worked only at the harshest setting: strongest lye, least ergot, two hours of hot boiling.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Quantifies the cost of the drugged-kykeon account: a careful multi-hour operation, not a bucket of barley left to soak.
treatment.strongestObjection: A single dataset; a replication might find a wider envelope.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Replication (TIK-R002) showing complete hydrolysis under milder conditions
Replication showing residual toxins even at these conditions

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: no admitted evidence record quotes the Results passage, and the second reader found TIK-E038 does not bear on it. A source is not evidence; the ledger records where the proposition is stated and has not admitted the observation behind it.

treatment.plainLanguage: The paper is said to report that another active ergot alkaloid, ergometrine, survived the process — but the ledger has not yet admitted the passage.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If it stands, the 'detoxified' preparation still contains a pharmacologically active co-product, which bears on safety and on what the drink would actually do.
treatment.strongestObjection: Until the passage is admitted, the ledger cannot say ergometrine persisted at all; and if it did, its pharmacological significance is an editorial note, not the paper's finding.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of an evidence record quoting the Results paragraph on ergometrine and ergometrinine
A pharmacological profile of the whole extract (TIK-R003) quantifying the residual alkaloid

claimAssessments.reasoning: Not anchor-only: TIK-E008 on the parent claim records the measured yield (0.54 and 0.48 mg per gram) and the authors' extrapolation that about 1 g per initiate could supply an active dose, and that basis carries the support given. The 0.5 mg minimum-effective-dose threshold is held on the anchor only, and the step is arithmetic on a single performance, not a measurement of effect.

treatment.plainLanguage: By the authors' arithmetic, about a gram of processed ergot would give the smallest dose of LSA reported to have any effect.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Links the chemistry to a servable dose, but a minimum effective dose is not a reliably visionary one; the dose gap remains.
treatment.strongestObjection: A threshold dose of a compound weaker than LSD, in a matrix with active co-products and nausea in the human record, is a long way from the experience the hypothesis needs.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of the dose-literature record behind the 0.5 mg figure
A pharmacological profile of the reconstructed preparation (TIK-R003, TIK-R013) at the one-gram dose

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor in the preprint alone, with no admitted evidence record; the ledger has not read the botanical or historical literature behind the naturalization date.

treatment.plainLanguage: The paper reports that the grasses hosting Claviceps paspali, a related ergot, reached Europe only in the nineteenth century.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true, it closes an alternative ergot route and makes the barley fungus plus lye the only pathway the drugged-kykeon account can use; if false, a different, possibly processing-free route would be available.
treatment.strongestObjection: An unevidenced botanical assertion in a chemistry paper's framing, by authors with a stake in the purpurea-plus-lye pathway.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of an evidence record on the naturalization history of the paspali host grasses
Evidence of Claviceps paspali or its hosts in classical Attica

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E012 qualifies: LSA is psychoactive but weaker than LSD, with nausea, autonomic effects and anxiety prominent in a human record dominated by morning-glory exposures; TIK-E013 shows pharmacological mystical experience is real for a different molecule. The reconstructed extract has never been profiled.

treatment.plainLanguage: Would the lye-processed drink actually give a profound, mostly positive vision at a servable dose? Nobody has tested it.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If the drink cannot deliver the experience, the drugged-kykeon account loses its motive even with the chemistry proven; if it can, the mechanism runs from fungus to phenomenology.
treatment.strongestObjection: LSA's human record is sedation, nausea and mixed effects, not reliable transcendence; the pennyroyal 'entourage' rescue is untested.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Pharmacological profile of the whole preparation (TIK-R003)
Co-administration test of pennyroyal constituents (TIK-R013)

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record evidences either side of the generator question: TIK-E013 shows a pharmacological route exists elsewhere, TIK-E019 documents the genre's inferential drift, and the proponents' premise of 'numerous accounts' (TIK-E040) is uncited beyond Pindar and Cicero on afterlife knowledge (TIK-E041). The ritual-sufficiency position is background, not evidence, and the phenomenon itself is under audit.

treatment.plainLanguage: Did initiates need a drug to have the experience — and did they report an experience at all?
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The pivot between the drugged-kykeon and ritual-machine accounts, and the point where the third account may dissolve the question.
treatment.strongestObjection: A rite stable for two millennia without a documented supply chain or dosing is exactly what a ritual machine predicts; and the transformative vision may be Kerényi's reading, not the ancients'.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Adversarial review of drug-free ritual induction (TIK-R007)
Philological audit of Phaedrus 250b–c and the testimonia (TIK-R011)

claimAssessments.reasoning: Indirect scaffolding only: TIK-E007 (Iberian analogue through citation) and TIK-E008 (feasible mechanism). Against it, the silent recipe (TIK-E015), the audited accounts (TIK-E016), and the methodological critique (TIK-E019); TIK-E009 records that no Eleusinian vessel has ever been tested. Lineage and funding records (TIK-E010, TIK-E027) are context.

treatment.plainLanguage: Was there processed ergot in the cup at Eleusis? Possible, never measured.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The Greek half stands or falls here; a lysergamide hit or a clean null in Eleusinian ceramics would decide it.
treatment.strongestObjection: The only recipe names nothing, the sanctuary's audited accounts record no drug, and the one place the claim could be tested has never returned a positive — because it has never been tested.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Lysergamide-targeted residue analysis of Eleusinian vessels (TIK-R001, TIK-R009)
Pontós primary text and re-analysis (TIK-R010, TIK-R004) showing the analogue diagnostic or background

claimAssessments.reasoning: No supporting record; TIK-E017 (McGovern) undermines, TIK-E021 shows the one drugged-cup text is fraud polemic, and TIK-E026/E027 record institutional capacity and funding as context. No early-Christian liturgical vessel has been chemically tested.

treatment.plainLanguage: Did some early Christian group, somewhere, put a drug in its communion cup? Untested.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A positive would establish a practice somewhere, not the original rite and not inheritance; a documented null would largely close the Christian half.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every early witness describes ordinary bread and wine, and the sole cup-manipulation text condemns a conjuring trick.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Preregistered residue survey of securely identified early-Christian vessels (TIK-R005)
A documentary witness describing an unusual ingredient outside heresiological polemic

claimAssessments.reasoning: The earliest documents describe bread and wine-with-water in Jewish thanksgiving form (TIK-E022, TIK-E023); the book's own scientific witness (TIK-E017) and a sympathetic reviewer (TIK-E020) reject the claim; the author declines to defend it (TIK-E024); TIK-E025 fixes the strong form as marketing. No record supports it.

treatment.plainLanguage: The Last Supper and the first Christians' rite were a psychedelic potion — every early document says otherwise.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The strong form of the inherited-sacrament account; its contradiction is what pushes the account back to its weak form.
treatment.strongestObjection: The witnesses are normative texts, a century or more after the events, describing the sanctioned rite rather than every community's practice.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Replicated psychoactive residues in first-century Eucharistic vessels
An early text, not polemical, describing a compounded cup as the norm

claimAssessments.reasoning: No direct record supports transmission; it stands on the lower rungs (TIK-C007 weakly supported, TIK-C009 mixed, TIK-C002) and shared wine-and-immortality symbolism. Every direct record undermines: McGovern (TIK-E017), Bremmer and Ehrman (TIK-E018), Brown (TIK-E020), and the author's own 'where are the drugs?' (TIK-E024). Not contradicted, because the Christian vessels are untested.

treatment.plainLanguage: A drugged sacrament passed from Greek mystery cults into the Christian cup — the grand thesis, running on symbolism.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The case's title claim; it requires both halves to hold and a chain between them, none of which is shown.
treatment.strongestObjection: Shared symbols need no transmission to explain — wine and immortality are the commonest religious imagery of the ancient Mediterranean — and the specialist fields reject the framework beneath it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An uncommon shared recipe appearing first in a mystery-cult vessel and later in a Christian one
Positive results from both TIK-R001 and TIK-R005

claimAssessments.reasoning: The Didache's berakah-form prayers (TIK-E023) and Justin's liturgy framed against the mysteries (TIK-E022) read as Second-Temple Jewish meal practice; two senior specialists reject the framework (TIK-E018). No record supports it.

treatment.plainLanguage: The Eucharist grew out of pagan mystery rites rather than Jewish meal blessings — the specialists say no, and the earliest texts look Jewish.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The framework the transmission claim inherits; if it falls, any future psychedelic Christian cup must supply its own vector.
treatment.strongestObjection: Expert consensus is not proof, and the scholars' full arguments are carried here only through journalism.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A demonstrated liturgical borrowing from a mystery cult in the earliest Eucharistic texts
An audit of the specialists' published arguments finding them weaker than quoted
